research_analysis.problem_statement: To prove a family of congruences for the sequence A028342, denoted as a(n), conjectured by Peter Bala. The congruences state that k | a(n + k) + a(n) for odd k, k | a(n + k) - a(n) for k ≡ 0, 2, 6 (mod 8), and k | 2(a(n + k) - a(n)) for k ≡ 4 (mod 8).
research_analysis.methodology: The proof utilizes a product congruence a(n + k) ≡ a(n)a(k) (mod k) derived through a group action of the cyclic group C_k, and computes a(p^r) mod p^r for each prime power by counting colored permutations fixed by a subgroup of order p, combining these via the Chinese remainder theorem.
research_analysis.experiments: The author checked Theorem 1.1 and the intermediate identities directly for all k up to 40 and all n up to 30.
research_analysis.findings: Successfully established the product congruence a(n + k) ≡ a(n)a(k) (mod k) and proved Bala's congruence conjecture for sequence A028342 across all three exhaustive residue classes of k modulo 8.

executive_summary: This paper successfully proves Peter Bala's congruence conjecture for the integer sequence A028342, which counts colored permutations. The research addresses a family of congruences governing the sequence terms a(n+k) and a(n) across three exhaustive residue classes of the modulus k modulo 8. To achieve this, the author develops an approach utilizing a group action of the cyclic group C_k on colored permutations to establish a key product congruence, stating that a(n+k) is congruent to a(n)a(k) modulo k. Furthermore, the methodology computes a(p^r) modulo p^r for prime powers by counting fixed points of subgroups, and subsequently applies the Chinese remainder theorem. The results definitively confirm Bala's conjectures, showing that k divides a(n+k)+a(n) for odd k, k divides a(n+k)-a(n) when k is congruent to 0, 2, or 6 modulo 8, and k divides twice the difference when k is congruent to 4 modulo 8. These theoretical findings were validated through direct computational checks for small values of n and k.
